# Uniform interval targets: exact feasibility and an obstruction

The proposed universal target statement is false already for n=d=1:
there need not exist an integer fiber carrying a uniform interval
probability measure nu such that nu(H)<=2 mu(H) for every closed ambient
halfspace. This is stronger than OC and its failure does not refute OC.

## An exact cumulative-function feasibility statement

Let the positive one-dimensional fibers be intervals I_j=[l_j,u_j], with
lengths w_j, and let M=sum_j w_j. Fix a positive-length integer fiber k.
For real t define

    L_k(t)=inf_s sum_j clip(t+s(j-k)-l_j,0,w_j),
    R_k(t)=inf_s sum_j clip(u_j-t-s(j-k),0,w_j),

where clip(v,0,w)=max(0,min(v,w)). These are the smallest unnormalized
left and right cap masses among all nonvertical halfspaces whose boundary
meets fiber k at continuous coordinate t.

There exists a nondegenerate uniform interval target in I_k with the
required domination if and only if both of the following hold:

1. k is a weighted median: sum_{j<k}w_j<=M/2 and sum_{j>k}w_j<=M/2.
2. There exist real a,b satisfying

       a l_k+b<=0, a u_k+b>=1,
       a t+b<=2L_k(t)/M whenever t in I_k and 2L_k(t)/M<1,
       a t+b>=1-2R_k(t)/M whenever t in I_k and 1-2R_k(t)/M>0.

The support inequalities imply a>=1/w_k>0. The target interval is then
[-b/a,(1-b)/a], and its cumulative distribution function is

    F(t)=clip(a t+b,0,1).

Proof. A vertical containing halfspace has target mass one, which gives
exactly the median requirements. Nonvertical halfspaces restrict to left
or right half-lines in fiber k. Their target masses are F(t) and 1-F(t),
including the endpoints because the uniform target has no atoms. Taking
the infimum over their slopes gives precisely

    F(t)<=2L_k(t)/M,  F(t)>=1-2R_k(t)/M.

For an upper bound strictly below one, clipping F is equivalent to the
displayed affine upper bound; for a lower bound strictly above zero it
is equivalent to the affine lower bound. Otherwise that inequality is
automatic. The support inequalities are exactly interval containment.
Thresholds outside I_k are covered by their endpoint inequalities and
monotonicity: L_k is nondecreasing and R_k is nonincreasing. This proves
necessity and sufficiency for every closed ambient halfspace.

This criterion is an exact finite linear feasibility problem in a,b.
Indeed for fixed t the mass is piecewise affine in slope s, with breaks

    s=(e-t)/(j-k), j!=k, e in {l_j,u_j}.

An infimum is therefore attained at one of these breaks or at one of the
two constant tail values as s tends to positive or negative infinity.
Substituting each candidate slope gives a continuous piecewise-affine
function of t, with finitely many pieces. The pointwise minimum of the
finite collection is again continuous piecewise affine. Consequently
L_k and R_k have that property on I_k.

For the affine upper inequalities it suffices to check the endpoints and
breakpoints of the closure of {t in I_k:2L_k(t)/M<1}; boundary constraints
are justified by limits from that set. Similarly use the closure of
{t in I_k:1-2R_k(t)/M>0} for the lower inequalities. Empty sets contribute
no constraints. On each remaining piece the difference of the two sides
is affine, so its endpoint inequalities suffice. For rational input
intervals all these finite coefficients are rational.

## A five-vertex rational obstruction

Take the convex polygon

    C=conv{(0,0),(3,0),(3,2),(2,4),(0,2)}.

Its four integer fibers at 0,1,2,3 are [0,2],[0,3],[0,4],[0,2]. Thus
M=11 and C is a full-dimensional compact convex body. Only k=2 is a
weighted median. Fibers 0,1,3 are excluded from target domination by the
vertical containing halfspaces z<=0, z<=1, z>=3, respectively, whose
masses are 2,5,2, all strictly below M/2.

Suppose a uniform interval J=[l,u] subset [0,4] in fiber 2 did satisfy
the domination. Put a=1/(u-l), b=-l/(u-l), so b<=0, and write
F(t)=clip(a t+b,0,1).

The halfspace

    H_R={x>=-z/2+7/2}

captures respective fiber lengths 0,0,3/2,0 and therefore mass 3/2.
Its threshold in the target fiber is 5/2. Domination gives

    1-F(5/2)<=3/11, or F(5/2)>=8/11.

The halfspace

    H_L={x<=4z-23/5}

captures respective fiber lengths 0,0,17/5,2 and mass 27/5.
Its threshold in the target fiber is 17/5. Domination gives

    F(17/5)<=54/55.

The first inequality implies l<5/2, and the second implies u>17/5.
Thus BOTH thresholds lie in the interval's linear-CDF portion. We obtain

    (5/2)a+b>=8/11,
    (17/5)a+b<=54/55,
    b<=0.

The first and third imply a>=16/55. Subtracting the first from the
second gives (9/10)a<=14/55, hence a<=28/99. This is impossible because

    16/55-28/99=4/495>0.

This excludes every possible target interval in every integer fiber.
In particular, no source-pairing scheme, fractional allocation, or other
transport can always produce such a uniform target: the obstruction
concerns the desired halfspace domination itself, before any restriction
on its construction. The general uniform-target route is therefore
blocked; specialized sufficient transport constructions remain valid.
